name: L7
label: Sub Pop
lede: Donita Sparks and Suzi Gardner named their band after slang for square. Then came riffs a wrestler used for his entrance music, a Prodigy cover, and the night Sparks dropped her jeans on British TV.

eras.title: Squares from Echo Park
eras.text: Sparks and Gardner start the band in LA's art-punk scene, lose a couple of drummers along the way, and don't get a lineup that sticks until Dee Plakas sits down behind the kit.

years.h: Two songwriters name their LA band after a word for square
years.p: Donita Sparks and Suzi Gardner start L7 out of the Echo Park art-punk scene. Sparks has said they wanted a name that didn't flag their gender.
years.xp:
Wikipedia dates the band to 1985. Sparks has called hearing Gardner's songs "one of the happiest days of my life", and says the two heard the same band in their heads.

Sparks has also said the band had no female role models growing up, and that letters from young women who picked up instruments because of L7 mean a lot to them.

years.h: Finch takes bass, Koutsky takes the drums
years.p: [[Jennifer Finch|add94f0b-8aba-4534-bda4-b1c6796b2d63]] and Roy Koutsky make it a four-piece, the lineup that cuts the first record.

years.h: A debut LP on Epitaph, and Koutsky leaves
years.p: L7 is fast, plain punk, made before the sludge set in.

years.h: Dee Plakas takes the drum stool and keeps it
years.p: Anne Anderson held the seat in between; her only studio trace is a cover of "Yummy Yummy Yummy" on SST's compilation The Melting Pot.
years.xp:
Anderson filled in after Koutsky's exit. Plakas's arrival gave L7 the lineup of Sparks, Gardner, Finch and Plakas that recorded everything through 1994.

Chicago Tribune critic Greg Kot later singled Plakas out as the band's secret weapon.

eras.title: Seattle noticed, then Slash called
eras.text: Sub Pop sees L7 in Seattle in 1989 and books them a day in a studio. Two years on, L7 have a Slash Records deal and a benefit show with Nirvana on the bill.

years.h: One day at Reciprocal, and L7 have a Sub Pop single
years.p: Sub Pop signs L7 after catching them in Seattle in 1989 and asks for a Singles Club 7-inch. They cut three tracks in a single day.
years.xp: Sub Pop's own history has Shove launching the Singles Club year in January 1990, set to "kick off the 1990's with a bang" and give L7 an underground hit. The other side, Packin' a Rod, came from the same day at Reciprocal Recording.

years.h: Smell the Magic gets four stars from Rolling Stone
years.p: A Singles Club buzz turns into a record. Rolling Stone calls it "one of Sub Pop's finest hours".
years.xp:
L7 went in to make an EP and it grew into a nine-song album. Sub Pop calls it "a landmark of '90s feminist rock", and its 30th-anniversary edition put all nine songs on one piece of vinyl for the first time, remastered.

Per Wikipedia, the record sits at No. 24 on Ugly Things magazine's list of the 40 best punk albums.

years.h: L7 turn up at Olympia's punk summit with a major-label deal
years.p: At the International Pop Underground Convention, L7 are the only band with major-label ties. Slash Records, a London Records subsidiary, has just signed them.
years.xp: Wikipedia notes L7 was the only act at the convention with major-label representation. Sub Pop had put them on the map a year earlier; the move to Slash was the first step out of the underground.

years.cap: L7 on stage at The Riverside, Newcastle
years.src: Wikipedia: Rock for Choice · Wikipedia: L7 (band)
yt: L7 and Nirvana, Rock for Choice, 10/25/91
years.h: Rock for Choice opens with Nirvana, Hole and Sister Double Happiness
years.p: L7 and LA Weekly music editor Sue Cummings build a Live Aid for abortion rights. The first night is October 25 at the Palace on Vine Street in Hollywood.
years.xp:
It started when Cummings interviewed L7 about a show they wanted to bill as "Rock Against Coat Hangers", with the money going to pro-choice groups. She pushed for something bigger, and the Feminist Majority Foundation became a key sponsor.

The series ran through 2001 and later brought in Pearl Jam, Foo Fighters, Rage Against the Machine and Ween. L7 eventually stepped back to focus on the band.

eras.title: Bricks, a tampon and no trousers
eras.text: Butch Vig produces the breakthrough, radio plays it for 13 weeks, and one year of mud and British television gives the tabloids more than they can print.

years.cap: L7 on stage at The Riverside, Newcastle, April 1992
years.h: Butch Vig takes the board on Bricks Are Heavy
years.p: [[Butch Vig|ba30915c-4d33-43c5-8c37-ead0b8061517]] has just finished Nevermind when Slash Records releases L7's first album with him. Rolling Stone later lists it among the essential recordings of the 1990s.
years.xp:
Shitlist found a second life in wrestling: Wikipedia reports Jon Moxley used it as entrance music through the mid-2000s, and Brian Pillman used it in ECW in 1996.

Wikipedia also reports the album sold 327,000 copies in the US by June 2000.

years.cap: Sparks at The Riverside, Newcastle, April 1992
years.h: "Pretend We're Dead" runs 13 weeks on US alternative radio
years.p: The single off Bricks Are Heavy peaks at No. 8 on the US Alternative chart and No. 21 in the UK.

years.h: Mud at Reading, and Sparks has an answer
years.p: What Sparks shouts at the crowd that has been pelting L7 all set. The airline had lost the band's pedals and there was no soundcheck.
years.xp:
Sparks told Guitar World the crowd was "just being assholes, throwing mud at us for the whole set", hitting the band's bodies and guitars. "It really felt like an assault, so I pulled my tampon out, and I threw it at them."

She described the hostility as having "a bit of a misogynist bend to it", and she has stood by the moment since.

years.h: Sparks drops her jeans on live British TV
years.p: During "Pretend We're Dead" on Channel 4's The Word, Sparks performs it bare from the waist down.
years.xp: Songfacts dates the broadcast to November 20, 1992. Sparks said the show already had a men's bum contest and a hidden camera in Oliver Reed's dressing room, so she "added" her own contribution to the craziness.

years.h: L7 wear pageant sashes at Rock for Choice, with Rage on the bill
years.p: The sold-out night in October has seven bands, including X, Firehose and Rage Against the Machine. L7's sashes name cities hit by anti-abortion violence.
years.xp: The previous September 27, the series had filled the Hollywood Palladium with L7, Exene Cervenka, the Red Hot Chili Peppers and Mudhoney.

years.h: Lollapalooza main stage, next to the Smashing Pumpkins and Beastie Boys
years.p: Hungry for Stink, with "Andres", reaches No. 117 on the Billboard 200. The bill also has Nick Cave and the Breeders.

yt: L7 as Camel Lips in Serial Mom
years.h: John Waters casts L7 as a band called Camel Lips
years.p: The band appears under that name in his 1994 film Serial Mom.

eras.title: A bass chair that won't sit still
eras.text: Finch leaves mid-album, Greenwood and then Tanaka take the bass, and L7 end up putting out a record on their own label before going quiet in 2001.

years.h: L7 share a Constitution Hall bill with Neil Young and Pearl Jam
years.p: A Voters for Choice benefit in Washington, D.C. Wikipedia reports Finch pulled her shirt off for the last song, causing a "slight fuss."

years.h: Finch leaves mid-album and Gail Greenwood takes the bass
years.p: Sparks and Greta Brinkman cover bass on The Beauty Process: Triple Platinum until Greenwood, ex-Belly, joins full time.

years.cap: L7 at the Emerson Theatre, Indianapolis, c. 1997
years.h: The Beauty Process arrives with a film by Novoselic
years.p: The fifth L7 album is the first with Greenwood on bass. [[Krist Novoselic|ac05e29f-0561-4445-bb26-5562d2389531]] directs the film that goes with it.
years.xp: The pseudo-documentary L7: The Beauty Process, directed by Novoselic, looks at a punk band in a pop market. The band also played Seattle's Bumbershoot that year.

years.h: The Prodigy put "Fuel My Fire" on The Fat of the Land
years.p: L7's original is on Hungry for Stink. The cover is on the Prodigy's 1997 album.

years.h: Slap-Happy comes out on L7's own Wax Tadpole label
years.p: To promote it, L7 fly banners over Lilith Fair ("Bored? Tired? Try L7.") and the Warped Tour ("Warped needs more beaver...love, L7").
years.xp: At Lilith Fair at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena on July 17, the banner read "Bored? Tired? Try L7." Greenwood left around this time, replaced by Janis Tanaka, ex-San Francisco's Stone Fox.

years.h: L7 go on indefinite hiatus
years.p: A note on the band's website says the future of the band is "a bit up in the air." Members scatter into side projects.
years.xp: Sparks and Plakas played in Donita Sparks and the Stellar Moments. Finch formed OtherStarPeople and later the Shocker. Tanaka played bass for Pink; Greenwood played with Bif Naked and reformed Belly.

eras.title: Back on Facebook, then back on stage
eras.text: Sparks rebuilds the fan base online, the reunion shows start in 2015, and L7 get a documentary, their first new song in 18 years and a Joan Jett-label album. In 2026, Jennifer Finch dies.

years.h: L7 announce they're back
years.p: Sparks had spent two years rebuilding the fan base on Facebook, one archive video at a time.
years.xp: The reunion began with archive posts on the band's Facebook page in 2012, and fans reassembled there. The announcement came December 10, 2014; the first shows followed June 6, 2015 at Rock am Ring in Germany, then Europe and Riot Fest in the US.

yt: L7: Pretend We're Dead, official trailer
years.h: Sarah Price's L7: Pretend We're Dead premieres in Los Angeles
years.p: The Kickstarter-funded documentary has interviews with Lydia Lunch, Shirley Manson, Krist Novoselic and Butch Vig.
years.xp: The film was nominated for a VO5 NME Award for Best Music Film. Original drummer Roy Koutsky died the same year, on February 15, at 53.

years.h: A 1990 Clutch Cargo's show, released 27 years late
years.p: Easy Action puts out Detroit (Live), recorded on the Smell the Magic tour on September 1, 1990.

years.h: L7 release their first new song in 18 years, aimed at Mar-a-Lago
years.p: "Dispatch from Mar-a-Lago," on Don Giovanni Records, takes its title from Donald Trump's Florida resort.
years.xp: The follow-up, "I Came Back to Bitch," arrived in February 2018.

years.h: Joan Jett's label puts out the first L7 album in 20 years
years.p: Blackheart Records issues Scatter the Rats after a PledgeMusic campaign, with "Burn Baby" as the lead single.
years.xp: Hyperallergic wrote that Sparks and Gardner still "pound out one solid, catchy, immediately identifiable power riff after another."

years.h: Bricks Are Heavy at 30, front to back
years.p: An 18-date tour plays the album in full, with a gold-and-black vinyl reissue remastered by Howie Weinberg.

years.h: L7 turn 40 at the Belasco in Los Angeles
years.p: The band's home-city anniversary show, on October 3.

years.src: Wikipedia: L7 (band) · Variety: Jennifer Finch · Rolling Stone: Jennifer Finch
years.h: Jennifer Finch dies at 59
years.p: L7 had announced their Last Hurrah tour in May. On July 13 Finch is diagnosed with brain cancer and withdraws, and she dies five days later.
years.xp:
Finch had been in L7 from 1986 to 1996 and again from the 2014 reunion. A GoFundMe for her medical costs and unreleased projects raised nearly $400,000, per Wikipedia.

Variety and Rolling Stone both ran the news of her death.
